newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD's Schroeder says Bonn will up taxes to make EMU.
newsitem.headline: SPD's Schroeder says Bonn will up taxes to make EMU.

text.p: A leader of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Friday that he thought Bonn would have to raise taxes to meet the entry criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Gerhard Schroeder, a potential candidate to challenge Chancellor Helmut Kohl in 1998 elections, said in an interview with broadcaster n-tv that Finance Minister Theo Waigel "wanted to raise taxes to make the euro-criteria."
Such a tax hike would be a "fatal mistake for the new currency," he said in an interview due to air on April 26.

Waigel on Friday introduced tax legislation to parliament which would round off a two-year plan to cut German tax bills by up to 30 billion marks a year from 1999 in a bid to boost investment and fight high unemployment.
But he faces a struggle to cut borrowing in the near term. He has not ruled out a spending freeze, tax hikes or a cut in welfare benefits to hit EMU targets.
Schroeder said he had doubts whether Germany could meet the strict fiscal guidelines as required this year, but did not specifically back a delay in the planned EMU launch in 1999.
"I think the failure of a rushed introduction would be more dangerous than a controlled delay," he said.
European Union nations that want to join EMU at the start must aim to limit budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product, according to the Maastricht Treaty.
Schroeder said a deficit of 3.1 percent of GDP would not be a catastrophe for the economy, but would not be good for building pulbic confidence in the euro.

He said he thought the euro would be positive in the long term, but would not create jobs in the short and medium term. A single currency would increase price pressure on Germany and its high social standards, he said.
